claim: In conditioned taste aversion (CTA) learning, animals can associate a novel taste with visceral nausea when the two stimuli are separated by several hours.
source: Here, we used conditioned taste aversion learning in the rat model, wherein animals associate a novel taste with visceral nausea
evidence: Supported by behavioral experiments showing CTA formation with inter-time intervals up to 8 hours, and cited literature on CTA paradigms.

claim: There are two parallel memory traces of a novel taste: a short-duration robust trace lasting approximately 3 hr, and a parallel long-duration weak trace lasting up to 8 hr.
source: demonstrate that there are two parallel memory traces of a novel taste: a short-duration robust trace, lasting approximately 3 hr, and a parallel long-duration weak one, lasting up to 8 hr, and dependent on the strong trace for its formation.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing two distinct clusters (1-3 hr and 4-8 hr ITI-CTAs) with different extinction patterns and different responses to weak US conditioning.

claim: The long-duration weak trace is dependent on the strong trace for its formation.
source: demonstrate that there are two parallel memory traces of a novel taste: a short-duration robust trace, lasting approximately 3 hr, and a parallel long-duration weak one, lasting up to 8 hr, and dependent on the strong trace for its formation.
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments showing that disruption of the NMDAR-CaMKII-AMPAR pathway during the short-trace period (within 3 hr) also disrupts long-trace CTA formation.

claim: Only the early robust trace is maintained by a NMDAR-dependent CaMKII-AMPAR pathway in the insular cortex.
source: Moreover, only the early robust trace is maintained by a NMDAR-dependent CaMKII- AMPAR pathway in the insular cortex.
evidence: Supported by biochemical data showing pT286CaMKIIα phosphorylation and GluA1 expression increases only during 0.5-3 hr after taste exposure, and pharmacological experiments showing that NMDAR, CaMKII, and AMPAR inhibition in IC affects short-trace but not long-trace CTA when applied after 3 hr.

claim: CTA was acquired after separating the taste and malaise stimuli for up to 8 hr but not 20 hr.
source: In agreement with previous findings, we found that CTA was acquired after separating the taste and malaise stimuli for up to 8 hr but not 20 hr (Figure 1B, Figure 1—source data 1 and Figure 1—figure supplement 1) (Kalat and Rozin, 1971; Kalat and Rozin, 1973; Rozin and Kalat, 1971; Revusky, 1971; Gutiérrez et al., 2003; Koh et al., 2009; Chinnakkaruppan et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data in Figure 1B showing significant aversion indices for 1-8 hr ITI-CTA groups but not 20 hr group, and cited previous literature.

claim: Non-parametric cluster analysis revealed two different clusters among 1–8 hr ITI-CTAs: 1–3 hr (short-trace) and 4–8 hr (long-trace) ITI-CTAs.
source: Interestingly, non-parametric cluster analysis revealed that there are two different clusters among 1–8 hr ITI-CTAs: 1–3 hr (hereinafter short-trace) and 4–8 hr (hereinafter long-trace) ITI-CTAs (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by statistical cluster analysis of behavioral data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Short-trace (1–3 hr) CTA groups exhibited a slower extinction pattern compared to long-trace (4–8 hr) CTA groups.
source: Consistent with the retrieval results, long-trace (4–8 hr) CTA groups exhibited a similar faster CTA extinction pattern, whereas short-trace (1–3 hr) CTAs exhibited a slower extinction. The long-trace CTAs were not different from an unpaired control group by extinction day4, in comparison with day7 aversion index (AI) in short-trace CTAs (Figure 1C and Figure 1—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by behavioral extinction data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Reverse conditioning (LiCl injection 1 hr before taste presentation) did not lead to taste aversion.
source: Reverse conditioning did not lead to taste aversion (Figure 1E), which indicates the importance of temporal order between taste and nausea in CTA learning.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The temporal order between taste and nausea is important for CTA learning.
source: Reverse conditioning did not lead to taste aversion (Figure 1E), which indicates the importance of temporal order between taste and nausea in CTA learning.
evidence: Inferred from the reverse conditioning experiment showing no CTA formation when US precedes CS.

claim: With a weak US (0.025M LiCl), CTA was formed following 1-4 hr ITI but not 5 hr ITI.
source: We thus conducted an ITI-CTA with a weak US (0.025M LiCl) to test whether weaker CTA learning can be acquired when an association is made during the short- (1–3 hr) but not the long-trace (4–8 hr) intervals. We found that CTA was formed following the short-trace intervals, and interestingly, also following a 4 hr but not 5 hr trace interval.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: There is a shift in the associability of the taste memory trace at around 3–4 hr after exposure to the taste stimulus.
source: Together these results suggest that there is a shift in the associability of the taste memory trace at around 3–4 hr after exposure to the taste stimulus (Figure 1D).
evidence: Inferred from the behavioral data showing different clustering patterns and the transition point in weak US experiments.

claim: Novel taste consumption increases CaMKIIα expression in the insular cortex 15 min after exposure.
source: We replicated the finding from the previous report (Figure 2—figure supplement 2), that 15 min after novel taste consumption, CaMKIIα expression is increased in the IC.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2 and cited previous report (Belelovsky et al., 2005).

claim: T286 phosphorylation of CaMKIIα (pT286CaMKIIα) was increased in the P2-fraction 30 min, 1 hr, and 3 hr following novel taste consumption, but not at 5 or 8 hr.
source: Interestingly, we observed that the T286 phosphorylation of CaMKIIα (pT286CaMKIIα) was increased in the P2-fraction 30 min following novel taste consumption, persisting for up to 3 hr (1 and 3 hr), but not 5 or 8 hr afterwards (Figure 2D,E and Figure 2—figure supplement 1,2).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: There was no significant difference in T305 phosphorylation of CaMKIIα (pT305CaMKIIα) between water control and novel taste groups at any time point.
source: There was no significant difference in T305 phosphorylation of CaMKIIα (pT305CaMKIIα; a phosphorylation site which prevents calcium/calmodulin activation of CaMKII) between water control and novel taste groups at any time point (Figure 2D–G and Figure 2—figure supplement 1,2).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The temporal dynamics of pT286CaMKIIα in the IC after novel taste experience corresponds to the short-trace timescale.
source: Intriguingly, the temporal dynamics of pT286CaMKIIα in the IC after the novel taste experience corresponds to the short-trace timescale, indicating a possible link between CaMKIIα and short-trace CTA learning.
evidence: Inferred from the correlation between pT286CaMKIIα phosphorylation duration (0.5-3 hr) and the short-trace behavioral window (1-3 hr).

claim: Novel taste experience-induced phosphorylation of T286CaMKIIα is NMDAR-dependent.
source: Therefore, we examined if NMDAR activation is necessary for novel taste-dependent CaMKIIα activation. Indeed, novel taste experience-induced phosphorylation of T286CaMKIIα is NMDAR-dependent, since i.p. injection of the NMDAR antagonist, MK801 (0.2 mg/kg b.w), 30 min before novel taste learning precluded phosphorylation of T286CaMKIIα in the IC (Figure 2H,I and Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2I demonstrating that MK801 blocks novel taste-induced pT286CaMKIIα increase.

claim: NMDAR in the insular cortex is dispensable for incidental taste learning but necessary for CTA learning.
source: Consistent with the literature, our data reveal that NDMAR in the IC is dispensable for incidental taste learning but necessary for CTA learning (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) (Rosenblum et al., 1997; Barki-Harrington et al., 2009; Parkes et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and cited literature.

claim: CaMKIIα in the insular cortex is dispensable for incidental taste learning but necessary for CTA learning.
source: We also found that CaMKIIα in the IC is dispensable for incidental taste learning but necessary for CTA learning (Figure 3—figure supplement 1,2).
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 and 2.

claim: Infusion of CaMKIIα inhibitor TatCN21 into the IC 25 min after taste consumption in 3 hr ITI-CTA conditioning attenuated CTA memory.
source: Next, we micro-injected CaMKIIα inhibitor TatCN21 or Tat control (Tatcont) into the IC 25 min from the beginning of the taste consumption in short-trace 3 hr ITI-CTA conditioning, and observed an attenuated CTA memory (Figure 3B and Figure 3—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Infusion of CaMKIIα inhibitor TatCN21 into the IC 25 min after taste consumption in 5 hr ITI-CTA conditioning attenuated CTA memory.
source: We micro-injected TatCN21 into the IC 25 min (i.e. short-trace timescale) from the beginning of the taste consumption in the long-trace 5 h ITI-CTA conditioning, and also observed an attenuated CTA memory (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: CaMKIIα inhibition in the IC 4 hr after taste consumption in 5 hr ITI-CTA conditioning had no effect on CTA memory.
source: However, consistent with the temporal dynamics of CaMKIIα phosphorylation in the IC, CaMKIIα inhibition in the IC 4 h after the taste consumption in the long-trace 5 hr ITI-CTA conditioning had no effect on CTA memory (Figure 3D).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: TatCN21 micro-infusion 2 hr after taste consumption in 3 hr ITI-CTA training did not significantly affect CTA memory.
source: To answer this, we performed a 3 hr ITI-CTA experiment in which we micro-infused CaMKIIα inhibitor TatCN21 2 hr after the taste consumption, and administered the LiCl 1 hr later. We observed a small non-significant effect (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: T286CaMKIIα phosphorylation in the IC is necessary for the development of the taste memory trace for association, and downstream targets play a vital role in maintaining the trace.
source: It is thus more likely that T286CaMKIIα phosphorylation in the IC is necessary for the development of the taste memory trace for the association and downstream target/s play a vital role in maintaining the taste memory trace for the CS-US association.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that CaMKIIα inhibition at 2 hr has minimal effect while inhibition at 25 min is effective, suggesting CaMKIIα acts early to establish the trace which is then maintained by downstream mechanisms.

claim: Experiencing novel taste increased total GluA1 but not pS831GluA1 in the synaptosomal fraction in the IC 1 hr later.
source: Indeed, experiencing novel taste increased total GluA1 but not pS831GluA1 or pS1303GluN2B in the synaptosomal fraction in the IC 1 hr later (Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There is a positive correlation between pT286CaMKIIα and GluA1 expression in animals sampling novel taste.
source: Linear regression analysis revealed a positive correlation between pT286CaMKIIα and GluA1 expression in animals sampling novel taste (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Novel taste-dependent increased GluA1 expression in the IC was precluded by TatCN21 microinjection into the IC.
source: To examine whether pT286CaMKIIα is required for the increased GluA1 expression in the P2-fraction after the taste consumption, we micro-infused CaMKIIα inhibitor TatCN21 into the IC 30 min before novel taste exposure and measured GluA1 expression 1 hr later. TatCN21 application reduced novel taste experience-dependent GluA1 expression in the P2-fraction (Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: NMDAR antagonist MK801 injection 30 min before novel taste reduced GluA1 expression.
source: Moreover, NMDAR antagonist MK801 injection 30 min before the novel taste also reduced GluA1 expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), indicating that NMDAR- and CaMKIIα-dependent increased synaptic expression of GluA1 in the IC mediates short-trace taste memory for the association with the US.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: NMDAR- and CaMKIIα-dependent increased synaptic expression of GluA1 in the IC mediates short-trace taste memory for the association with the US.
source: Moreover, NMDAR antagonist MK801 injection 30 min before the novel taste also reduced GluA1 expression (Figure 4—figure supplement 3), indicating that NMDAR- and CaMKIIα-dependent increased synaptic expression of GluA1 in the IC mediates short-trace taste memory for the association with the US.
evidence: Inferred from the combined findings that NMDAR and CaMKIIα are required for GluA1 upregulation and that this pathway is necessary for short-trace CTA.

claim: Microinjection of AMPAR antagonist CNQX into the IC 1 hr after taste consumption in 3 hr ITI-CTA conditioning attenuated CTA memory.
source: Microinjection of AMPAR antagonist, CNQX, (1 μl/hemisphere; 3 nM/μl) (Tse et al., 2011) into the IC 1 hr after the taste consumption in short-trace 3 hr ITI-CTA conditioning attenuated the CTA memory (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4D and cited methodology.

claim: CNQX micro-injection into the IC 2 hr after taste consumption in 3 hr ITI-CTA learning attenuated CTA memory.
source: Interestingly, CNQX micro-injection into the IC 2 hr after the taste consumption in 3 hr ITI-CTA learning also attenuated CTA memory (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Microinjection of CNQX into the IC 1 hr after taste consumption in 5 hr ITI-CTA conditioning attenuated CTA memory.
source: Furthermore, microinjection of CNQX into the IC 1 hr (short-trace timescale) after the taste consumption in long-trace 5 hr ITI-CTA conditioning also attenuated the CTA memory (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: CNQX micro-injection 4 hr after novel taste consumption in 5 hr ITI-CTA had no effect on CTA.
source: However, in accordance with the timescale of short-trace and CaMKIIα-GluA1 activation, we found that CNQX micro-injection 4 hr after novel taste consumption in 5 hr ITI-CTA had no effect on CTA (Figure 4G).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4G.

claim: Inhibition of CaMKIIα or AMPAR in the IC during short-trace timescale attenuated both short-trace and long-trace CTA memory.
source: It is intriguing that the inhibition of CaMKIIα or AMPAR in the IC during short-trace timescale attenuated short-trace CTA memory. In addition, inhibition of the CaMKIIα-GluA1 pathway during short-trace timescale also attenuated long-trace CTA.
evidence: Supported by the combined behavioral data from Figures 3 and 4 showing effects of TatCN21 and CNQX on both short-trace and long-trace CTA when applied during the short-trace window.

claim: Long-trace CTA was not affected when CaMKIIα-GluA1 pathway in the IC was left intact for 3 hr.
source: However, long-trace CTA was not affected when CaMKIIα-GluA1 pathway in the IC was left intact for 3 hr.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data showing no effect of CaMKIIα or AMPAR inhibition when applied 4 hr after taste in 5 hr ITI-CTA.

claim: There are two parallel taste memory traces subserved by different mechanisms: one that is robust but decays quickly, and another which is weak but lasts longer.
source: Together, these data reveal that there are two parallel taste memory traces which are subserved by different mechanisms: one that is robust but decays quickly, and another which is weak but lasts longer.
evidence: Inferred from the combined behavioral, biochemical, and pharmacological data showing distinct temporal profiles and molecular requirements for short-trace vs long-trace CTA.

claim: NMDAR-CaMKIIα-AMPAR in the IC are not necessary for incidental taste learning and memory.
source: It is important to note that NMDAR-CaMKIIα-AMPAR in the IC are not necessary for incidental taste learning and memory, whereas muscarinic receptors are critical for incidental taste learning (Ferreira et al., 2002; Parkes et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by pharmacological experiments and cited literature showing differential molecular requirements for associative vs non-associative taste learning.

claim: Different molecular mechanisms take place in the insular cortex to mediate associative and non-associative taste learning and memory.
source: It is interesting that different molecular mechanisms take place in the same cortex, the insular cortex, to mediate associative and non-associative taste learning and memory.
evidence: Inferred from the finding that NMDAR-CaMKIIα-AMPAR pathway is required for CTA but not incidental taste learning, while muscarinic receptors are required for incidental taste learning.

claim: Different pharmacological manipulations (APV, TatCN21, CNQX) in the IC when applied within 3 hr after CS presentation only modify but not completely erase CTA memory.
source: We should emphasize that different pharmacological manipulation (APV, TatCN21, CNQX) in the IC when applied within 3 hr after the CS presentation only modifies but not completely erases the CTA memory.
evidence: Observed from the behavioral data showing partial rather than complete disruption of CTA following pharmacological interventions.

claim: Several previous reports demonstrate that pharmacological perturbations in the IC during CTA conditioning only partially disrupt CTA memory, and the disrupted CTA appears similar to long-trace CTA memory.
source: It is also noteworthy that several previous reports demonstrate that pharmacological perturbations in the IC during CTA conditioning only partially disrupt CTA memory, and that the disrupted CTA appears similar to long-trace CTA memory (Rosenblum et al., 1993; Rosenblum et al., 1997; Berman et al., 2000; Eisenberg et al., 2003; Gutiérrez et al., 2003; Barki-Harrington et al., 2009; Inberg et al., 2013; Stern et al., 2013; Parkes et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple cited studies showing similar patterns of partial CTA disruption.

claim: Over time, there is a transformation from taste memory trace dominance (short-trace) and IC dependency to multiple memory traces (long-trace) due to multi-channeled background experience.
source: Thus, it is possible that over time, there is a transformation from the taste memory trace dominance (i.e. short-trace) and IC dependency to multiple memory traces (i.e. during long-trace) due to the multi-channeled background experience, e,g., time, space, food digestion-dependent body physiology, etc.
evidence: Speculative interpretation based on the observed differences between short-trace and long-trace CTA and the partial effects of IC manipulations.

claim: Animals exhibit higher preference to a taste hours following the first-time experience, supporting the learned safety theory.
source: First, in support of the learned safety theory, and in line with the previous reports, we found that animals exhibit higher preference to the taste hours following the first-time experience (Figure 3—figure supplement 4) (Kalat and Rozin, 1973; Gutiérrez et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 4 and cited literature.

claim: The hippocampus is critical to assimilate the episodic component in CTA.
source: Second, with regards to background interference theory, we propose that the multi-channeled background information can be viewed as episodic components and that, for example, the hippocampus is critical to assimilate the episodic component in CTA (Chinnakkaruppan et al., 2014; Koh et al., 2009).
evidence: Proposed based on cited studies showing hippocampal involvement in CTA.

claim: The robust short-trace fades within 3 hr in the IC but the long-trace, which is weak, lasts longer.
source: Third, in line with the trace decay theory, our findings demonstrate that the robust short-trace fades within 3 hr in the IC but the long-trace, which is weak, lasts longer.
evidence: Supported by the temporal profile of pT286CaMKIIα phosphorylation and the behavioral differences between short-trace and long-trace CTA.

claim: The non-linear decay of the short trace suggests that it dominates over the long trace, so that when the former fades, the latter is revealed.
source: Moreover, the non-linear decay of the short trace suggests that it dominates over the long trace, so that and when the former fades, the latter is revealed (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Inferred from the behavioral patterns and proposed in the model shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: CTA learning may engage multiple memory systems to take part in the long-trace associative process.
source: We propose a multiple memory trace theory, wherein we suggest that CTA learning may engage multiple memory systems to take part in the long-trace associative process and that after experiencing the taste, the IC plays a critical role during short-trace (Figure 4—figure supplement 5).
evidence: Proposed theoretical framework based on the experimental findings and illustrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 5.

claim: Protein acetylation, phosphorylation, and induction of proteins were observed in the IC many hours following novel taste consumption.
source: For instance, protein acetylation, phosphorylation, and induction of proteins were observed in the IC many hours following novel taste consumption, and it is possible that these correlative molecular changes (proteins synthesis and epigenetic regulation) may contribute to the long-trace CTA (Swank and Sweatt, 2001; Yefet et al., 2006; Elkobi et al., 2008; for reviews see Gal-Ben-Ari and Rosenblum, 2012).
evidence: Supported by cited studies showing various molecular changes in IC following taste learning.

claim: Short-trace CTA complies with Hebbian plasticity involving NMDAR-CaMKII-AMPARs in the IC probably in coordination with the amygdala.
source: Conceptually, on the one hand, our short-trace CTA complies with the commonly held assumption of neuroscience theories of associative learning that convergence of CS and US information onto particular cells/circuits leads to changes in synaptic strength at the synapses mediating the CS input to those commonly activated cells/circuit and that it underlies association formation, i.e. Hebbian plasticity (NMDAR-CaMKII-AMPARs in the IC probably in co-ordination with the amygdala; Yasoshima et al., 2000; Ferreira et al., 2005; Hashikawa et al., 2013).
evidence: Interpreted based on the experimental findings and cited literature on Hebbian mechanisms and amygdala involvement.

claim: Long-trace CTA challenges the Hebbian assumption, and homeostatic plasticity may play a crucial role to encode multiple memory traces via coordinating several brain structures.
source: On the other hand, the long-trace CTA challenges this assumption, and it is possible that because of the multi-channeled background information with an increasing time interval as discussed above, homeostatic plasticity may play a crucial role to encode multiple memory traces via coordinating several brain structures such as the IC, amygdala, hippocampus, prefrontal cortices in the long-trace CTA (Vitureira et al., 2012; Turrigiano, 2012; Pozo and Goda, 2010).
evidence: Speculative proposal based on the experimental findings and cited literature on homeostatic plasticity.

claim: The neural mechanisms of associative learning can be an assimilation of multiple memory traces when the two relevant experiences are separated in time.
source: Overall, our data suggest that the neural mechanisms of associative learning can be an assimilation of multiple memory traces when the two relevant experiences are separated in time.
evidence: Concluded from the overall experimental findings showing different mechanisms for short-trace vs long-trace CTA.

claim: Temporal contiguity has a vital influence on associative learning.
source: Thus, in essence, these theories mention that temporal contiguity has a vital influence on associative learning.
evidence: Stated based on the historical theories of Thorndike and Pavlov discussed in the introduction.

claim: The inter-time-interval (ITI) between the CS (novel taste) and the US (visceral information) in the CTA paradigm can last for hours.
source: For example, the inter-time-interval (ITI) between the CS (novel taste) and the US (visceral information) in the conditioned taste aversion (CTA) paradigm can last for hours (Garcia et al., 1955; 1985; Kalat and Rozin, 1971; 1973; Chambers, 1990; Rosenblum et al., 1993; 1997; Yamamoto et al., 1995; Hashikawa et al., 2013; Adaikkan and Rosenblum, 2012; Stern et al., 2013; Inberg et al., 2013; Chinnakkaruppan et al., 2014; Parkes et al., 2014; Sano et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by multiple cited studies on CTA paradigms.

claim: The long ITI between CS and US in CTA is reasonable from physiological, ecological, and evolutionary perspectives due to the digestion and absorption process.
source: The long ITI between CS and US in CTA is reasonable from physiological, ecological, and evolutionary perspectives. The minutes to hours process of digestion followed by absorption may dictate the animal to associate between the taste consumed and its delayed physiological consequences (for more information see reviews, Gal-Ben-Ari and Rosenblum, 2012; Kong and Singh, 2008).
evidence: Explained based on biological reasoning and cited reviews.

claim: Micro-injection of the protein synthesis inhibitor anisomycin into the insular cortex within 3 hr but not 4 hr after taste inhibits associative taste memory in the latent inhibition of CTA paradigm.
source: This observation is further supported by the previous demonstration that micro-injection of the protein synthesis inhibitor, anisomycin, into the insular cortex (IC) within 3 hr but not 4 hr after the taste inhibits associative taste memory in the latent inhibition of CTA paradigm (Merhav and Rosenblum, 2008).
evidence: Supported by cited study showing time-dependent effects of protein synthesis inhibition.

claim: CaMKIIα has the potential to store information through auto-phosphorylation at T286, which can act as a molecular positive feedback loop.
source: Given ample evidence that novel taste experience impacts the phospho-proteome in the IC (see reviews, Adaikkan and Rosenblum, 2012; Gal-Ben-Ari and Rosenblum, 2012) and the idea that calcium calmodulin-dependent protein kinase II (CaMKII) has the potential to store information (Lisman, 2014 and the references therein), we aimed to test the possibility that CaMKIIα, through auto-phosphorylation (at T286; which can act as a molecular positive feedback loop), maintains the taste memory trace in the IC.
evidence: Based on cited literature and established knowledge about CaMKII function.

claim: Novel taste experience significantly increased pY1472GluN2B compared to water controls.
source: Consistent with a previous report (Barki-Harrington et al., 2009), novel taste experience significantly increased pY1472GluN2B compared to water controls (T (10) = -2.319, p=0.046).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and cited literature.

claim: pS1303GluN2B phosphorylation was not different between water and novel taste groups.
source: Interestingly, however, pS1303GluN2B phosphorylation, which is known to be regulated by CaMKIIα, was not different from water and novel taste groups (T (35) = -1.078, p=0.288).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The control group exhibited taste aversion of about 36% upon the second taste encounter (Test1), and demonstrated less aversion on the third taste encounter.
source: The control group from the main Figure 1B, which exhibited taste aversion of about 36% upon the second taste encounter (Test1), demonstrated less aversion on the third taste encounter (paired t-test between Test1 and Test2; T = 4.781, p=0.001).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Rats demonstrated high aversion to a novel palatable taste upon sampling for the first time (neophobia), but exhibited less aversion upon the second and third encounter (attenuation of neophobia).
source: Rats demonstrated high aversion to a novel palatable taste upon sampling for the first time. This is referred to as neophobia, i.e., reluctance to consume a novel taste due to lack of knowledge regarding the post-ingestive consequences. However, rats exhibited less aversion upon the second and third encounter, demonstrating that taste preference is an adaptive process. This phenomenon is called attenuation of neophobia.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The CTA control group upon Test1 did not differ from Test2 of attenuation of neophobia group, indicating that ingesting a taste only once is not sufficient to determine that the taste is completely safe.
source: As expected, the CTA control group upon Test1 (i.e. second time consumption of the novel taste) did not differ from Test2 of attenuation of neophobia group (T (19) = 0.954, p=0.352), indicating that ingesting a taste only once is not sufficient to determine that the taste is completely safe to consume and thus rats need to ingest the same taste at least three times to form a memory that the taste is completely safe.
evidence: Supported by behavioral comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Microinjection of NMDAR antagonist APV into the IC 25 min after consumption of novel taste in 1 hr ITI-CTA conditioning with weak US attenuated CTA memory.
source: We micro-injected the NMDAR antagonist into the IC 25 min from the beginning of the taste consumption in 1 hr ITI-CTA conditioning with a weak US and observed an attenuated CTA memory, consistent with a previous report in which a strong US was administered (Rosenblum et al., 1997; but also see Ferreira et al., 2002) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3A and cited literature.

claim: APV micro-infusion 4 hr after taste consumption in 5 hr ITI-CTA conditioning did not affect CTA memory.
source: Intriguingly, we did not observe any effect when we made a similar manipulation in the IC 4 hr after the taste consumption in 5 hr ITI-CTA conditioning with a strong US (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B; all the remaining experiments were done with a strong US).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Infusion of CaMKIIα inhibitor TatCN21 into the IC 30 min before 1 hr ITI-CTA conditioning disrupted CTA memory.
source: Infusion of CaMKIIα inhibitor TatCN21 into the IC 30 min before 1 hr ITI-CTA conditioning disrupted CTA memory.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Infusion of NMDAR antagonist APV into the IC 30 min before 1 hr ITI-CTA conditioning disrupted CTA.
source: Infusion of NMDAR antagonist APV (10 μg/μl) into the IC 30 min before 1 hr ITI-CTA conditioning disrupted CTA.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: TatCN21 infusion 30 min before novel taste consumption did not affect incidental taste memory.
source: TatCN21 infusion 30 min before novel taste consumption did not affect the incidental taste memory.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: APV infusion 30 min before novel taste consumption did not affect incidental taste memory.
source: APV infusion 30 min before novel taste consumption did not affect the incidental taste memory.
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Micro-infusion of AMPAR antagonist CNQX 30 min before taste learning did not affect incidental taste memory.
source: Micro-infusion of AMPAR antagonist CNQX 30 min before the taste learning did not affect the incidental form of the appetitive taste memory (T (14) = 0.335, p=0.743).
evidence: Supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4.
